common_name: Purple de Oro Daylily (Reblooming Compact Purple Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Purple de Oro is a purple-flowered sport of the classic Stella de Oro, sharing the same compact, heavily reblooming habit.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Purple de Oro arose as a color sport of the landmark reblooming daylily Stella de Oro, keeping the same compact size, tough constitution, and near-constant rebloom from late spring through frost, but trading the golden-yellow flowers for ruffled plum-purple blooms with a contrasting gold-green throat. It tolerates heat, humidity, drought, and average soil with equal ease, needing only routine deadheading of spent scapes to keep it tidy. Its small scale and long bloom season make it a dependable choice for borders, mass edging, and mixed containers, and it combines well with the yellow-flowered Stella de Oro for a two-tone reblooming daylily planting. Clumps can go many years between divisions; divide only when flowering noticeably declines from overcrowding.

common_name: Mini Stella Daylily (Dwarf Reblooming Golden Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Mini Stella is a dwarfer, smaller-flowered relative of Stella de Oro, well suited to edging and container growing.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Mini Stella takes the reblooming, compact model of the landmark daylily Stella de Oro and scales it down further, with a smaller overall plant size and daintier golden-yellow flowers that suit small-space edging, rock gardens, and containers better than the somewhat larger Stella de Oro. Like its relative, it blooms continuously from late spring through frost rather than in a single flush, and tolerates heat, humidity, drought, and average soil with equal ease. Deadhead spent scapes to keep the planting tidy and encourage continued rebloom; clumps are long-lived and rarely need dividing except to control size or propagate new plants.

common_name: Pandora's Box Daylily (Award-Winning Miniature Eyed Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; Pandora's Box is a miniature-flowered daylily bred by Talbott and released in 1980, long a favorite for its sharply contrasting eye zone.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Pandora's Box is an award-winning miniature daylily with cream-colored petals set off by a sharply defined, deep cranberry-purple eye zone around the throat, a striking contrast that has kept it a long-standing garden favorite since its 1980 introduction. The small (under 3 inch), abundant flowers open over a compact, well-branched scape, giving a long, floriferous bloom season typical of the best miniature daylilies. Like other daylilies it tolerates heat, humidity, and average to poor soil with ease once established, needing only routine deadheading of spent scapes to keep the planting tidy. Clumps are long-lived and multiply steadily; divide every four to six years when flowering begins to decline from overcrowding.

common_name: Fire and Ice Hosta (White-Centered Green-Margin Hosta)

planting.note: Plant container stock or divisions in spring in rich, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade to full shade; Fire and Ice is a sport with a bold white-centered leaf and a narrow, irregular dark-green margin, one of the most widely sold variegated hostas.

directions: Plant in rich, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade to full shade, avoiding direct hot afternoon sun which can scorch the white center. Fire and Ice is one of the most dramatic and widely grown variegated hostas, with narrow, pointed leaves dominated by a bold, nearly pure-white center bordered by a thin, irregular dark-green margin — the strong color contrast makes it a standout accent or edging plant even from a distance. Pale lavender flowers appear on tall scapes in mid- to late summer. Because so much of the leaf lacks chlorophyll, it grows a bit more slowly and stays smaller than solid-green hostas of similar parentage, and it benefits from consistent moisture and protection from slugs, which tend to target the softer white tissue. A dependable, high-contrast choice for brightening a dark shade bed.

planting.note: Plant container stock or divisions in spring in rich, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade; Fragrant Bouquet was named the American Hosta Growers Association Hosta of the Year in 1998 and is grown as much for its unusually large, sweetly fragrant flowers as for its foliage.

directions: Plant in rich, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade with some morning sun to help the wide creamy-white leaf margins develop their best color. Fragrant Bouquet is a large, vigorous hosta with broad, glossy, chartreuse-green leaves edged in a wide, creamy-white margin, named the American Hosta Growers Association Hosta of the Year in 1998. Its real claim to fame, unusual among hostas, is its flowers — large, pure-white, and genuinely sweetly fragrant, opening on tall scapes in mid- to late summer and carrying a scent noticeable from several feet away, unlike the faint or absent fragrance of most hosta flowers. It forms a substantial, well-proportioned mound over a few seasons and combines well with blue or dark-leaved hostas for foliage contrast. Provide consistent moisture and protect young growth from slugs in spring.
sources: American Hosta Growers Association — Hosta of the Year

planting.note: Plant container stock or divisions in spring in rich, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade; Shade Fanfare was bred by hosta pioneer Paul Aden and released in 1986, and colors best with a bit more morning sun than most hostas need.

directions: Plant in rich, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade, giving it a bit more morning sun than most hostas need to bring out its best color contrast. Shade Fanfare, a 1986 introduction from noted hosta breeder Paul Aden and a sport of the older cultivar Flamboyant, has heart-shaped, softly corrugated chartreuse-green leaves broadly edged in creamy white, with pale lavender flowers on tall scapes in summer. It forms a neat, well-proportioned mound and has proven itself over decades as a reliable, widely available variegated hosta for the front or middle of a shaded border. Provide consistent moisture, especially during the heat of summer, and protect emerging spring growth from slugs, which favor the tender new foliage.

common_name: Regal Splendor Hosta (Frosty Blue Cream-Margined Hosta)

planting.note: Plant container stock or divisions in spring in rich, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part to full shade; Regal Splendor is a Walters Gardens introduction and sport of the classic vase-shaped Krossa Regal, named Hosta of the Year in 2003.

directions: Plant in rich, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part to full shade, giving it plenty of room to reach its full, substantial size. Regal Splendor, named Hosta of the Year in 2003, is a sport of the classic Krossa Regal, keeping the same tall, upright, vase-shaped habit and frosty blue-gray leaf color prized in that older cultivar, but adding a creamy-yellow margin around each leaf for extra contrast. Its strongly vertical form and large scale make it an excellent architectural accent or centerpiece for a shaded bed, distinct from the low, spreading mounds of many other hostas. Pale lavender flowers appear on tall scapes in mid-summer, held well above the foliage. Provide consistent moisture through the growing season and protect emerging spring growth from slugs.
sources: American Hosta Growers Association — Hosta of the Year
